title: When does the Moon set on Thursday?
description: {{NAME_4}} sees the Moon set at ten at night on Monday, and the video finds how many hours later it sets on Thursday by multiplying the days by five sixths of an hour, the same way as the example in the book. It ends by checking the answer against the three days.
teaching_notes: One idea: the same delay each day adds up, so three days of five sixths of an hour is three times five sixths. Watch for students who count four days from Monday to Thursday.

source: {{NAME_4}} saw the Moon setting on Monday at 10 pm. {{NAME_4}}'s mother, who is a scientist, told {{NAME_4}} that every day the Moon sets 5/6 hour later than the previous day. How many hours after 10 pm will the moon set on Thursday?
video_script.why: The child has multiplied a whole number by a fraction and now uses it to add the same delay again and again over the days.
video_script.substitution: Three days of the same delay of five sixths of an hour add up to three times five sixths of an hour.
video_script.anchor: The Moon sets five sixths of an hour later each day, and sets at ten at night on Monday: how many hours later on Thursday?
video_script.payoff_line: The Moon sets two and a half hours after ten at night, at half past midnight

final_answer.value: 5/2 hours (2 1/2 hours) after 10 pm, so the Moon sets at 12:30 am
final_answer.spoken: two and a half hours after ten at night, at half past midnight

video_script.fraction_reading: one sixth, five sixths, fifteen sixths, five halves

names.{{NAME_4}}: watches the Moon set each night

maths_rules: Monday to Thursday = 3 days of delay
check: each delay is less than 1 hour, so 3 delays are less than 3 hours
video_script.design: One idea: the same delay each day is repeated, so multiply the delay by the number of days. A night clock at ten with three jumps of five sixths of an hour is the anchor and stays all video; the working band builds in the idea part.

beats.on_screen: small title card From your book; a night sky with the Moon setting; a clock at 10 on Monday; a question mark at Thursday

marks.scene: the small title card From your book appears
marks.mon: the night sky and the clock at ten on Monday appear
marks.mum: the words 5/6 hour later each day appear on the board
marks.ask: a question mark appears at Thursday

narration: <bookmark mark='scene'/>This is a question from your book about {{NAME_4}} and the Moon.
<bookmark mark='mon'/>{{NAME_4}} saw the Moon set on Monday at ten at night.
<bookmark mark='mum'/>{{NAME_4}}'s mother is a scientist. She says that each day the Moon sets five sixths of an hour later than the day before.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>How many hours after ten at night will the Moon set on Thursday?

beats.on_screen: the question stays on the board; Keeko sits at the corner of the board

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: a clock face with one hour cut into six equal parts; a jump of five of those parts is marked as the delay of one day

marks.hour: one hour of the clock is cut into six equal parts
marks.jump: a jump of five parts is marked as the delay of one day

narration: <bookmark mark='hour'/>Picture one hour cut into six equal parts, each one sixth of an hour.
<bookmark mark='jump'/>Each day, the Moon sets five of these parts later than the day before.

beats.on_screen: Given: Moon sets at 10 pm on Monday; delay each day = 5/6 hour

marks.given: the given lines are written in the working band

narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, the Moon sets at ten at night on Monday.
Each day it sets five sixths of an hour later than the day before.

beats.on_screen: To find: hours after 10 pm when the Moon sets on Thursday

marks.find: the find line is written under the given lines

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find how many hours later the Moon sets on Thursday.

beats.on_screen: Step 1: Monday to Thursday = 3 days of delay (Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday)

marks.days: the days Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday are marked after Monday

narration: <bookmark mark='days'/>Step one, count how many times the Moon moves later.
Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday each add one delay, so there are three delays.
<bookmark mark='mult'/>Step two, multiply three by five sixths of an hour.
Do it the same way as the example in your book.
<bookmark mark='count'/>Three times five is fifteen, so we count fifteen parts of one sixth.

beats.on_screen: Step 3: 6/6 = 1 hour, so 12/6 = 2 hours, and 3/6 hour is left

marks.twelve: 12/6 = 2 hours, and 3/6 hour left, is written

narration: <bookmark mark='six'/>Step three, change the sixths into hours, because six sixths make one hour.
<bookmark mark='twelve'/>Twelve sixths make two hours, and three sixths of an hour are left.

beats.on_screen: Step 4 (check): each delay is less than 1 hour, so 3 delays are less than 3 hours; 2 hours and 3/6 hour fits

marks.check: each delay is marked as less than one hour
marks.fits: the total of 2 hours and 3/6 hour is marked as less than 3 hours

narration: <bookmark mark='check'/>Step four, check the total against the three days.
Each delay is less than one hour, so three delays are less than three hours.
<bookmark mark='fits'/>Two hours and three sixths of an hour fits.

beats.on_screen: Answer: 15/6 = 5/2 = 2 1/2 hours after 10 pm, so the Moon sets at 12:30 am
narration: <bookmark mark='hours'/>Fifteen sixths is five halves, which is two and a half hours.
<bookmark mark='pay'/>The Moon sets two and a half hours after ten at night, at half past midnight.
